newsitem.title: USA: Farrakhan supporters gather outside U.N..
newsitem.headline: Farrakhan supporters gather outside U.N..

text.p: Fiery Nation of Islam minister Louis Farrakhan told a rally of tens of thousands of supporters on Wednesday that the "bestial people" of the United States led the world in murder, crime and rape.

In a speech lasting two hours and 45 minutes outside the United Nations, the black militant minister accused the global organisation of failing to stand up to the United States, which he called "a bully" and its policies "evil."
"America leads the world in murder, in rape, in crime, in drug addiction, in prostitution," he said. "You are the most unrefined, uncultured and bestial people on the earth."
The rally, called by its organisers a "World's Day of Atonement," came on the first anniversary of Farrakhan's Million Man March in Washington.
Farrakhan, widely criticised for his controversial trips to Libya, Cuba, Sudan and Iraq, took sharp aim at other nations.
Echoing the tone of the Million Man March, when he berated black men for failing to live up to their potential, he used this forum to accuse rulers of failing to act as leaders.
Instead, he said, they profit from economic embargos, weapons production and international arms sales.
"Our light has gone out," he said. "The condition of the people got wasted on our watch."

Farrakhan spoke from behind bullet-proof glass, stepping outside only briefly to bow to the crowd's cheers. "I have a lot of friends here, but I also have a lot of vicious enemies that would love to see something evil happen to me," he said.
Police estimated the crowd at less than 38,000 people. Organisers estimated the gathering, which unlike last year included women and children, at as many as 200,000 people.
About 20 blocks of midtown Manhattan were closed to traffic. Streets were transformed into a bazaar of peddlers hawking t-shirts, buttons and tapes of Farrakhan's speeches.
Many women in the enthusiastic crowd wore long flowing white robes, while many men wore the dark suits and bow ties distinctive of Farrakhan's followers.
The rally had sparked anger among many Jews who consider Farrakhan anti-Semitic. One Jewish group had hoped to stage a counter-protest but was denied a police permit.

"The bizarre world odyssey from one tyranny to another, from one terrorist capital to another only reinforced our concerns about Mr. Farrakhan, what he believes and what he represents," said American Jewish Committee executive director David Harris.

In a highly controversial trip to Libya this year, Farrakhan received a $250,000 human rights award, a possible violation of U.S. law that bans financial dealings with Libya due to its alleged sponsoring of iterrorism.

He asked that Libya be allowed to make the award, calling it "a downpayment on an expiation from sins." He also called for an end to trade embargos against Cuba and Iraq and proposed that a fact-finding team be sent to explore allegations of slavery in Sudan.
South African politician Winnie Mandela also appeared on stage but stood silently as a spokesman said she had been asked not to speak by the South African government.
